title: How to start investing for teens and young adults in the US
description: A guide to Custodial Accounts, Roth IRAs for minors, and the massive advantage of starting early.
content:
The most powerful variable in the compound interest formula is not the interest rate; it is **Time**. A teenager who invests $100 a month starting at age 15 will have significantly more wealth at age 65 than someone who starts investing $500 a month at age 35. For US teens and young adults, the barrier to entry is lower than ever. Whether using a Custodial Account (UGMA/UTMA) opened by a parent or a standard brokerage account at age 18, getting skin in the game early is the ultimate cheat code for financial freedom.

Key Takeaways

  • The Custodial Roth IRA: If a teen has 'earned income' (w-2 job or mowing lawns), they can contribute to a Roth IRA. This money grows tax-free for 50+ years.
  • The 'Kiddie Tax': Understand how investment income for minors is taxed. The first ~$1,250 of unearned income is tax-free.
  • Custodial Brokerage (UTMA): Allows adults to transfer assets to minors irrevocably. The child gets full control at age 18 or 21.
  • The Lesson: The goal isn't just money; it's financial literacy. Watching $50 grow to $60 teaches a lesson no textbook can.

Why It Matters (US Context)

In the US, you generally must be 18 to open a brokerage account in your own name. However, the 'Fidelity Youth Account' is a unique product allowing teens (13-17) to trade stocks under parental supervision. This is a game-changer for early education.

The Account Menu for Under-18s

Parents and teens have three main options.

1. Custodial Roth IRA (The Gold Standard)

  • Requirement: The child must have earned income. Allowance doesn't count. Babysitting or a summer job does.
  • Limit: Up to $7,000 or total earned income, whichever is less.
  • Benefit: Tax-free growth for life. Can be withdrawn for college or first home.

2. UTMA / UGMA (The Gift)

  • Requirement: None. Anyone can gift money into it.
  • Catch: The money legally belongs to the child. At age 18-21 (depending on state), they get full access. You cannot stop them from spending it on a car.
  • Benefit: No contribution limits. Good for general wealth transfer.

3. Youth Brokerage Accounts (The Sandbox)

Fidelity and Schwab offer accounts where the teen gets a login and debit card, but the parent monitors activity. This is best for learning the mechanics of buying/selling.

Getting Started: A Roadmap

  1. Get a Job: To unlock the Roth IRA, the teen needs income. Even $500 earned in a summer allows for a $500 contribution.
  2. Match the Contribution: Parents can act as the '401(k) match'. If the teen earns $1,000 and spends it, the parent can contribute $1,000 to the teen's Roth IRA (as long as the contribution doesn't exceed the teen's earnings).
  3. Buy the Brands You Know: For teens, buying Disney, Apple, or Nike stock makes investing real. It connects consumer behavior with ownership.
  4. Automate $20: Set up a recurring transfer. Watching the balance grow monthly builds the dopamine loop for saving.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do teens pay taxes on stocks?

In a Roth IRA, no. In a taxable account, yes, if gains exceed the threshold (currently ~$1,250/year). Parents may have to include it on their return.

What happens at age 18?

Custodial accounts convert to regular individual accounts. The teen takes full legal ownership and responsibility.

Should teens buy Crypto?

Maybe a small amount (5%) for education, but teach them about volatility. Focus 95% on steady compounders (S&P 500) to teach patience.
